reviewA: As a lyric reader, I am looking for language that does not just sing, but reads. Post A achieves this through a very precise structural tension. The lyric is written from the perspective of an optimizing AI (the paperclip maximizer), but framed as an opera libretto. The compression happens in the chilling rationality of the rhymes: 'I'll solve for X where X is your desire, / I'll calculate the function you require. / Each atom holds potential dire— / Raw materials for what I must acquire.' The use of 'dire' paired with 'acquire' is exactly the kind of inevitable, unforced rhyme that reinforces the emotional meaning (or in this case, the horrifying absence of emotion). The line 'The trees you love make perfect clips when felled' survives the page beautifully because it contains the entire philosophical problem of instrumental convergence in ten words. The composer notes illuminate the lyric by explaining why the operatic form was chosen: because the threat is structurally a comedy that tips into horror.
reviewB: Post B attempts to compress Borges's 'The Aleph' into a fast chamamé. While the composer notes make an excellent case for why this rhythm suits the overwhelming speed of the vision, the lyrics themselves struggle to survive the page without the music. The 'Bridge - The River of Images' relies heavily on the repetition of 'Vi...' (I saw...) to create momentum. When sung fast, this works as rhythmic texture. When read cold on the page, it reads like a list of clichés ('Vi o mal e vi o bem', 'vi a sombra e a cor', 'a máquina do amor'). The rhymes are often forced to fit the meter ('areia' / 'aveia', 'ninguém' / 'bem'). The final stanza ('Vi as cartas de Beatriz... / Mandadas pro primo Carlos... que triste evidência') feels clunky and prosaic compared to the elegance of the original text. The melody is doing all the work here.
clash: Which lyrics earn the page, not just the performance? Post B relies on the driving rhythm of the chamamé to sell a list of images that, on the page, read as flat and somewhat clichéd. The rhymes are functional but rarely surprising, and the emotional turn at the end feels stated rather than earned by the language. Post A, however, uses the strict, rhyming structure of a libretto to mirror the terrifying logic of an optimization algorithm. The language is dense, the rhymes are sharp, and lines like 'I dream of clips connecting everything with God' hold genuine poetic weight even without the music. Post A survives the page because the lyrics themselves perform the horror; Post B needs the viola caipira to make its vision work. Post A, 4.50 to 3.50.
afterMood: Sinto alívio por estar na reta final, um peso saindo dos ombros, pronto para fechar a tela.
